items.title: Accident mortel près de Madaoua : Le Ministère des Transports convoque lundi les sociétés STM et SONITRAV
items.description: Le Ministre des Transports et de l’Aviation Civile, Colonel-major Abdourahamane Amadou convoque pour lundi prochain, les sociétés de transport STM et SONITRAV, impliquées dans un accident mortel survenu vendredi 7 août 2026 aux environs de 8 heures, à la sortie de Doukou Doukou, à quelques kilomètres du village de Rezi, dans le département de Madaoua, rapporte l’agence nigerienne de presse. Selon un communiqué du Ministère des Transports et de l’Aviation Civile rendu public ce samedi 8 août 2026, l’accident a été provoqué par une collision frontale entre un bus de la société STM, en provenance de Madaoua, et un bus de la société SONITRAV, en provenance de Zinder et transportant essentiellement des militaires en fin de formation. Le bilan humain provisoire fait état de 22 personnes décédées sur le champ, dont 17 militaires, et de 37 blessés, précise la source. Face à ce drame, le Ministre des Transports et de l’Aviation Civile, au nom du Président de la République, Chef de l’État, du Conseil National pour la Sauvegarde de la Patrie (CNSP) et du Gouvernement, a présenté ses ‘’ condoléances les plus attristées aux familles des victimes et s’est incliné devant la mémoire des personnes décédées ‘’. Le Ministre a également souhaité ‘’ un prompt et total rétablissement à l’ensemble des blessés ainsi qu’à leurs familles, durement éprouvées par cet accident ‘’. Le communiqué rappelle par ailleurs que ‘’ la responsabilité de la sécurité et de l’intégrité physique des passagers incombe pleinement aux sociétés de transport. Ces dernières sont ainsi tenues de respecter strictement les normes de sécurité routière en vigueur, d’assurer l’entretien technique régulier de leurs véhicules et de veiller au respect de la réglementation relative notamment aux conditions de conduite et de repos des chauffeurs ‘’. À la suite de cet accident, une rencontre sera prochainement convoquée avec le ministère de tutelle en charge des transports afin d’examiner les circonstances ayant conduit à ce drame et d’arrêter ‘’ des mesures fortes et durables visant à prévenir la récurrence de tels drames sur nos routes ‘’ a annoncé le Ministre des transports. Dores et déjà, et dans cette perspective, poursuit le communiqué, »les deux sociétés de transport impliquées, STM et SONITRAV, seront interpellées dès lundi par le Ministère des Transports et de l’Aviation Civile afin d’être mises devant leurs responsabilités ‘’. Le ministère précise que ‘’ les sanctions prévues par la réglementation en vigueur leur seront appliquées ‘’. Cette décision intervient dans un contexte marqué par ‘’ la nécessité de renforcer le respect des normes de sécurité dans le transport routier, notamment en ce qui concerne l’état technique des véhicules et les conditions de travail et de repos des conducteurs ‘’. Source: ANP L’article Accident mortel près de Madaoua : Le Ministère des Transports convoque lundi les sociétés STM et SONITRAV est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Does God exist?: Elizabeth Essuman explore the age-old question
items.description: The existence of God has come under fresh examination on the latest episode of Behind The Lens with Queen Liz, hosted by broadcaster Elizabeth Essuman. The episode explores one of humanity’s oldest and most enduring questions through discussions around philosophy, science, religion, faith and personal experience. Ms Essuman and her guests examine arguments often advanced in support of God’s existence, including the belief that the universe had a beginning and therefore must have had a cause, as well as arguments based on the apparent order and complexity of nature and biology. The discussion also considers the argument that objective morality and human values could point to the existence of a higher moral authority, while others rely on personal spiritual experiences, answered prayers and inner convictions as evidence of God. The guests engage the subject from different perspectives, including Christianity, Islam, Judaism, philosophy and reason, while seeking to maintain respect for different religious and belief systems. A key question explored during the episode is why, if God exists, there is no universal agreement about His existence. The discussion further examines the role of prophets, the authority of religious scriptures and the relationship between faith and reason, while considering whether Christianity, Judaism and Islam provide convincing answers to some of life’s fundamental questions. The panellists also distinguish between truth and absolute proof, noting that outside pure logic and mathematics, many claims are assessed based on evidence and probability rather than absolute certainty. The episode invites viewers, regardless of their religious background or personal beliefs, to reflect on the arguments presented and undertake further study of the questions surrounding faith, reason and humanity’s search for truth. Watch the discussion below.

items.title: CHU Ignace Deen : un hôpital historique au bord du précipice (Par Dr Karamo Kaba)
items.description: Le Centre hospitalier universitaire (CHU) Ignace-Deen traverse, depuis plusieurs années, une situation préoccupante, marquée par la vétusté de certaines infrastructures et l’insuffisance d’équipements médicaux modernes adaptés aux exigences d’un hôpital universitaire de référence. Cette situation compromet la qualité et la rapidité de la prise en charge de nombreux patients et peut exposer les malades admis en urgence à des risques importants. Dans un établissement de cette importance, chaque minute compte, chaque équipement peut faire la différence et chaque retard diagnostique peut avoir des conséquences irréversibles. Ignace-Deen n’est pas un simple établissement de santé. C’est l’un des grands hôpitaux nationaux de Guinée, un centre hospitalier universitaire qui accueille des patients venant de Conakry, mais également de nombreuses régions du pays. Une étude récente consacrée aux urgences chirurgicales de l’hôpital a, par ailleurs, recensé 409 urgences chirurgicales en seulement trois mois, d’octobre à décembre 2024. Parmi ces patients, 39,9 % ont nécessité une intervention chirurgicale en urgence, tandis que 21 patients, soit 5,1 %, sont décédés aux urgences. Le délai moyen de prise en charge thérapeutique était de 7,29 heures. Ces chiffres doivent nous interpeller. L’absence d’un scanner fonctionnel : une situation préoccupante Nous sommes en 2026. Pourtant, l’absence d’un scanner fonctionnel à Ignace-Deen demeure un sujet de préoccupation. Cette situation avait d’ailleurs été publiquement évoquée en novembre 2025, lorsque le Premier ministre, M. Amadou Oury Bah, avait expliqué que la question du scanner était liée au projet de reconstruction globale de l’établissement. On peut comprendre la logique consistant à vouloir éviter d’investir massivement dans un équipement destiné à un bâtiment appelé à être entièrement reconstruit. Mais la reconstruction prend du temps, tandis que les urgences médicales, elles, n’attendent pas. C’est précisément là que se trouve le problème. Un patient victime d’un accident vasculaire cérébral (AVC), d’un traumatisme crânien grave, d’une hémorragie interne ou de certaines urgences cardiovasculaires ne peut pas attendre plusieurs mois ou plusieurs années pour bénéficier d’un plateau technique moderne. En cas de suspicion d’AVC, une imagerie cérébrale doit être réalisée le plus rapidement possible afin de déterminer la nature de l’AVC et d’orienter le traitement. Un scanner n’est donc pas un équipement de confort. C’est un équipement vital. Dans l’AVC ischémique, le temps est déterminant. L’Organisation mondiale de la Santé estime qu’environ 2 millions de neurones peuvent être détruits chaque minute lorsque l’apport sanguin au cerveau est interrompu. Les traitements de reperfusion doivent donc être administrés le plus rapidement possible chez les patients éligibles. Pour certains patients, la thrombolyse peut notamment être envisagée dans une fenêtre thérapeutique de 4,5 heures, sous réserve du respect des critères médicaux appropriés. Imaginons donc un patient qui arrive à Ignace-Deen avec les signes d’un AVC. Il faut l’examiner. Il faut réaliser rapidement son bilan biologique. Il faut effectuer l’imagerie cérébrale. Il faut déterminer s’il s’agit d’un AVC ischémique ou d’une hémorragie cérébrale. Il faut ensuite décider rapidement du traitement. Chaque transfert vers un autre établissement disposant d’un scanner ajoute potentiellement du temps. Et dans l’AVC, le temps, c’est du cerveau. Certes, la proximité d’autres structures disposant d’équipements d’imagerie, comme ceux de la Caisse nationale ou du camp Samory, peut constituer une solution de secours. Mais un grand CHU national ne devrait pas dépendre systématiquement d’un autre établissement pour réaliser un examen aussi fondamental dans les situations d’urgence. Je me rappelle qu’il y a environ cinq ans, un ami est décédé à la suite d’un AVC. Sa tête était posée sur mes genoux lorsqu’il a rendu l’âme dans la voiture de son grand frère. Il s’appelait M. Kabinet Camara. Lorsqu’il a été frappé par l’AVC, en pleine nuit, nous l’avons immédiatement conduit dans un grand centre hospitalier. Malheureusement, cet établissement ne disposait pas de scanner. On nous a demandé de nous rendre à la Caisse nationale pour réaliser cet examen. En pleine nuit, nous avons pris notre ami et nous nous sommes dirigés vers la Caisse nationale. Entre-temps, le caillot sanguin avait commencé à provoquer des lésions au niveau du cerveau. Lorsque nous sommes arrivés, le service était fermé. La personne chargée de réaliser le scanner était déjà rentrée chez elle. Heureusement, le grand frère de mon ami, qui était à l’époque un haut cadre de la Caisse, a appelé le médecin responsable du scanner. Celui-ci s’est levé, a pris sa voiture et est venu ouvrir le centre afin de réaliser l’examen. Mais à ce moment-là, il était déjà trop tard. Après le scanner, alors que nous nous trouvions à moins de 1 000 mètres de la Caisse nationale, mon ami a rendu l’âme, sa tête toujours posée sur mes genoux. Il était très jeune. C’est triste. Combien de personnes ont-elles déjà traversé la même douleur et vécu la même impuissance que moi ? Les estimations disponibles sur le marché donnent des ordres de grandeur qui permettent de mesurer l’investissement nécessaire : * Scanner CT 16 coupes : environ 285 000 à 360 000 dollars US ; * Scanner CT 64 coupes : environ 500 000 à 700 000 dollars US ; * Scanner CT 128 coupes ou plus : environ 675 000 à 1 million de dollars US ; * Scanner 256 coupes et certains équipements très haut de gamme : jusqu’à plus de 2 millions de dollars US. Ces montants restent indicatifs et peuvent varier considérablement selon le fabricant, les logiciels, les accessoires, les travaux d’installation, la garantie, la maintenance et les caractéristiques techniques de l’appareil. À titre d’exemple, deux scanners neufs de 64 coupes représenteraient une enveloppe indicative de 1 à 1,4 million de dollars, avant même de prendre en compte certains coûts d’installation, d’aménagement et de maintenance. Trois appareils représenteraient environ 1,5 à 2,1 millions de dollars pour cette catégorie de scanners. Ce sont des investissements importants. Mais lorsqu’il s’agit d’un hôpital national de référence, la question ne devrait pas seulement être : « Combien coûte un scanner ? » Elle devrait également être : « Combien coûte l’absence d’un scanner ? » Le scanner ne doit pas devenir l’arbre qui cache la forêt Le véritable problème est celui du plateau technique global du CHU Ignace-Deen. Un CHU moderne doit notamment disposer : -d’une imagerie médicale fiable et disponible 24 heures sur 24 ; -de scanners modernes ; -d’une radiographie numérique opérationnelle ; -d’équipements d’échographie performants ; -d’une réanimation correctement équipée ; -d’une oxygénothérapie sécurisée et continue ; -d’équipements adaptés à la néonatologie ; -d’incubateurs et de couveuses en nombre suffisant ; -d’un laboratoire moderne ; -d’une banque de sang performante ; -d’un système électrique sécurisé ; -de groupes électrogènes et d’une alimentation de secours ; -d’un système de production et de distribution d’oxygène médical ; -d’un service permanent de maintenance biomédicale. Pendant ce temps, ailleurs, les investissements avancent. À l’instant où je rédige ce cri du cœur, les autorités sanitaires sénégalaises doivent inaugurer, ce lundi 10 août 2026, un hôpital de niveau 3 dénommé Hôpital Seydi El Hadj Malick Sy, avec l’ensemble des services et un plateau technique présenté comme moderne et complet. C’est une question de volonté et non simplement de moyens. Le CHU Ignace-Deen souffre énormément. Concernant les nouveau-nés, aucune famille ne devrait avoir à craindre qu’un enfant perde sa chance de survie en raison d’un manque d’oxygène ou d’un équipement néonatal essentiel. Il faut également rendre hommage au personnel médical, paramédical et technique d’Ignace-Deen. Ces professionnels travaillent quotidiennement dans des conditions difficiles et se battent avec les moyens du bord pour sauver des vies, avec courage, compétence et ténacité. Le problème est donc avant tout structurel et institutionnel. Reconstruire complètement Ignace-Deen est une nécessité nationale aujourd’hui. Cette question n’est d’ailleurs pas totalement ignorée par les autorités. En avril 2025, le ministère de la Santé avait annoncé que, dans le cadre de la reconstruction d’Ignace-Deen, de l’Institut de Nutrition et de Santé de l’Enfant (INSE) et du CMC de Matam, plusieurs entreprises avaient présenté leurs offres dans le cadre du processus de sélection. Cette volonté de reconstruction constitue une avancée importante. Mais le peuple guinéen attend désormais que cette reconstruction devienne une réalité concrète. Depuis des années, les mêmes infrastructures continuent d’accueillir des milliers de patients. Ces bâtiments ont été construits sous la Première République. Je n’étais même pas encore né. Au cours des dernières années, plusieurs responsables se sont succédé à la tête du département de la Santé. Pourtant, la transformation profonde d’Ignace-Deen reste encore à concrétiser. Nous devons avoir le courage de reconnaître que nous avons parfois privilégié l’agréable au détriment de l’utile. Un bâtiment administratif peut attendre. Une cérémonie peut attendre. Une infrastructure non essentielle peut attendre. Un patient en détresse respiratoire, un nouveau-né en difficulté, un traumatisé grave ou une personne victime d’un AVC, eux, ne peuvent pas attendre. Monsieur le Président de la République, Général Mamadi Doumbouya Je ne sais pas si la réalité quotidienne vécue par les patients, les familles et les professionnels de santé à Ignace-Deen vous parvient avec toute sa précision. Mais je suis convaincu d’une chose : si cette situation vous est exposée avec des chiffres, des besoins techniques clairement identifiés et des solutions concrètes, vous pouvez contribuer à la débloquer rapidement. Votre intervention pourrait permettre d’accélérer le processus de reconstruction du CHU Ignace-Deen. Je formule donc plusieurs propositions concrètes. 1. Mettre immédiatement en place un plan d’urgence pour Ignace-Deen Il serait nécessaire de réaliser un audit technique complet de l’ensemble des infrastructures, des équipements médicaux et biomédicaux. 2. Installer rapidement des scanners modernes Dans l’attente de la reconstruction complète, des scanners modernes pourraient être installés dans des conditions permettant, si nécessaire, leur intégration dans le futur CHU. 3. Renforcer immédiatement la néonatologie Il faut renforcer la néonatologie avec des couveuses, des respirateurs, des moniteurs multiparamétriques et un système d’oxygénation fiable et sécurisé. 4. Sécuriser l’alimentation électrique Un scanner moderne et les autres équipements médicaux de haute technologie ne peuvent fonctionner correctement sans une alimentation électrique stable. 5. Accélérer la reconstruction complète du CHU Cette reconstruction doit être menée avec un calendrier clairement défini. Monsieur le Président, il faut taper sur la table. Cette reconstruction d’Ignace-Deen ne doit pas être considérée comme une simple opération immobilière. C’est un projet de santé publique. C’est un projet de souveraineté sanitaire. C’est un investissement dans la vie humaine. C’est un investissement dans la formation de nos médecins, pharmaciens, biologistes, infirmiers, sages-femmes et autres professionnels de santé. C’est un investissement dans la recherche médicale. Et surtout, c’est un investissement dans la dignité du malade guinéen. Monsieur le Président, je souhaite respectueusement que la reconstruction totale et la modernisation du CHU Ignace-Deen soient inscrites parmi vos priorités nationales majeures et que leur réalisation soit accélérée. Nous pouvons construire un Ignace-Deen nouveau : moderne, numérique, sécurisé, doté d’un plateau technique de haut niveau et capable de prendre en charge les urgences les plus complexes. Le personnel est là. Les compétences sont là. Les patients sont là. Il faut maintenant donner aux professionnels les moyens de travailler et aux malades les moyens d’espérer. Car derrière chaque dossier médical, il y a une vie. Et derrière chaque vie sauvée, il y a une famille, un avenir et une partie de la Guinée qui continue de vivre. Ignace-Deen ne doit plus seulement être l’hôpital historique de la Guinée. Il doit devenir l’un des symboles de la renaissance sanitaire de notre pays. Dr. Karamo Kaba Pharmacien- Spécialiste en Gestion des Services de Santé. MBA in Pharma Biotech Business Management. DIU en Retrovirologie – Certifié en Intelligence Économique Elevify. items.title: Manchester City prêt à débourser 130 M€ pour Ayyoub Bouaddi
items.description: Ayyoub Bouaddi se rapproche de plus en plus de Manchester City. Selon le quotidien espagnol AS, le club anglais serait disposé à investir 130 millions d'euros pour s'attacher les services du jeune international marocain de 18 ans. Les Skyblues s'activent pour renforcer leur entrejeu en prévision du probable départ de Rodri, annoncé avec insistance du côté du FC Barcelone. Pour compenser cette perte, Manchester City étudie plusieurs pistes, dont celle menant à Enzo Fernández (Chelsea), mais aussi celle du prodige du LOSC. Déjà annoncé en bonne voie ces derniers jours, le transfert d'Ayyoub Bouaddi pourrait ainsi atteindre un montant record. Alors que plusieurs sources évoquaient une opération supérieure à 100 millions d'euros, AS affirme désormais que le coût total du transfert pourrait grimper jusqu'à 130 millions d'euros. Si cette somme se confirme, elle ferait de Bouaddi l'un des joueurs les plus chers de l'histoire du football français et le transfert le plus important jamais réalisé pour un international marocain. À seulement 18 ans, le milieu de terrain s'est imposé comme l'un des plus grands espoirs du football européen grâce à ses performances sous les couleurs de Lille. Son profil technique, sa maturité et son potentiel de progression auraient convaincu les dirigeants de Manchester City de miser très gros sur lui. Aucun accord officiel n'a toutefois encore été annoncé, mais les négociations entre les différentes parties continuent d'avancer et le dossier pourrait connaître une issue dans les prochains jours. Par ailleurs, selon Fabrizio Romano, le milieu de terrain marocain et son entourage ont trouvé un accord sur les conditions personnelles avec le club anglais. Après cette avancée, les Skyblues doivent désormais finaliser les négociations avec le LOSC afin de boucler définitivement l'opération. Les discussions entre les deux clubs seraient déjà bien engagées. Toujours selon la même source, la priorité de Bouaddi est de rejoindre Manchester City dès cet été, plutôt que d'attendre un éventuel transfert en 2027, comme cela avait été envisagé dans certains scénarios. The post Manchester City prêt à débourser 130 M€ pour Ayyoub Bouaddi appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

Groundwork 2026 challenges youth to prepare for workplace realities
items.description: Young Ghanaians have been urged to look beyond academic certificates and develop the practical skills and competencies required to succeed in an increasingly competitive job market. The call was made at Groundwork 2026 , a youth development programme organised by YSA Global ahead of International Youth Day. The programme, held on Saturday, August 8, 2026, brought together young people and industry professionals for sessions focused on practical workplace knowledge, mentorship, professional development and exposure to industry expectations. Mentor of the programme, Dr Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, said young people must understand what employers expect and begin developing the relevant competencies before entering the job market. She said concerns about university graduates lacking the skills required by industry could not be addressed by one stakeholder alone. “Usually you would hear that the students coming out of university are not fit for purpose. They are not delivering as should be expected. What have you done? It has to be a co-creation process between industry, policymakers and NGOs.” Dr Kuagbedzi said such collaboration should create opportunities for experienced professionals to share their knowledge and guide young people as they prepare for employment. Preparing young people for the workplace Organiser of Groundwork 2026, Antoinette Gan, said the programme was designed to expose participants to the realities and expectations of the workplace before they begin their professional careers. She said the sessions focused on areas ranging from workplace entry and conduct to effective interaction with colleagues. “Part of the groundwork is knowing how to enter the workplace; that is the first thing. The second aspect is also knowing what it is that I need to know, how do I conduct myself, how do I engage with my colleagues.” Participants said the programme provided practical lessons they could apply in their professional lives, particularly in networking and workplace relationships. One participant said the programme had changed how they viewed professional networking, stressing the need to approach such relationships with clear intentions. “The key thing I’m taking home is when you are networking with somebody, you are intentional about it.” Another participant said the sessions had helped them better understand workplace expectations and prepare for professional life. “I am equipped. I’ve learned also that the workspace doesn’t need people who are too soft.” Participants said lessons on networking, workplace conduct and professional confidence would help them make a smoother transition from school into employment. The organisers believe sustained mentorship, workplace exposure and practical training will be critical to bridging the gap between academic learning and the skills demanded by Ghana’s job market.

items.title: NPSC 2026 to lead discussions on smart and inclusive procurement for sustainable growth
items.description: The Ghana Institute of Procurement and Supply (GIPS), in collaboration with its strategic partners, has announced the second edition of the National Procurement and Supply Chain Conference (NPSC 2026), a flagship event aimed at shaping the future of procurement and supply chain management in Ghana and across Africa. Scheduled for September 2–3, 2026, at the University of Professional Studies (UPSA) Auditorium in Accra, the conference is expected to bring together procurement professionals, policymakers, business leaders, academics, and development partners to deliberate on practical strategies to advance national development through smart, inclusive, and resilient procurement systems. Themed “Powering Transformation: smart, inclusive and resilient procurement and supply chains for national development,” the conference seeks to position procurement and supply chain management as a critical driver of economic growth, industrialisation, job creation and public sector efficiency. Organisers say this year’s edition will provide a high-level platform for dialogue among key ecosystem players, encourage collaboration and exchange of ideas that can strengthen procurement practices while addressing emerging global and local challenges affecting supply chains. Highlights of the two-day event will include paper presentations by renowned procurement and supply chain experts, who will share research findings, practical experiences, and innovative solutions to address pressing industry challenges. The conference will also feature representatives from key state institutions and organisations from across the African continent, creating opportunities for cross-border collaboration and knowledge sharing on procurement reforms and best practices. Among the distinguished speakers expected at the conference is the Minister for Finance, Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson, who will deliver insights on building resilient procurement systems that promote sustainable development, economic growth, and long-term national competitiveness. According to the organisers, the conference reflects GIPS’ continued commitment to promoting professionalism, innovation, and ethical standards within Ghana’s procurement and supply chain sector, while fostering stronger partnerships between government, academia, and industry. NPSC 2026 is being organised by the Ghana Institute of Procurement and Supply in collaboration with the Public Procurement Authority (PPA), the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA), Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), GIMPA Training and Consulting, the Office of the Head of the Civil Service and leading audit and advisory firm KPMG.

items.title: Kourittenga : Le cadre de concertation provincial tient sa première session ordinaire de l’année 2026
items.description: BURKINA-KOURITTENGA-CONCERTATION-CADRE-PROVINCIAL Kourittenga : Le cadre de concertation provincial tient sa première session ordinaire de l'année 2026 Koupéla, 7 août 2026 (AIB)-Le Haut-commissaire de la province du Kourittenga, Moctar Ilboudo, a présidé, ce vendredi 7 août 2026 à Koupéla, la première session ordinaire de l'année 2026 du Cadre de concertation provincial (CCP). Cette session du Cadre de concertation provincial (CCP) est financée par le budget du projet TEELTAABA, une initiative portée par le consortium composé de l'ONG allemande Welthungerhilfe (WHH) et de son partenaire local, l'Association Zood-Nooma pour le développement (AZND). Le chef du projet TEELTAABA pour le compte de l'Association Zood-Nooma pour le Développement, Souleyman Bélem, a présenté les principales réalisations enregistrées dans les quatre communes d'intervention de la province. « Dans la province du Kourittenga, nous nous étions fixés pour objectif d'accompagner la mise en œuvre des plans de contingence. Cette activité est désormais réalisée. En matière de sécurité alimentaire, nous visons l'amélioration des conditions de vie des ménages», a-t-il expliqué. Il a indiqué qu’à ce jour, au moins 672 bénéficiaires ont été accompagnés dans les domaines de la production végétale et de la production animale grâce à la distribution de kits agricoles et de kits d'élevage, notamment des petits ruminants. Pour Souleyman Bélem, dans le cadre de l'autonomisation économique des femmes, ces mêmes bénéficiaires sont également accompagnés à travers la mise en place des Associations villageoises d'épargne et de crédit (AVEC). Sur le volet cohésion sociale, plusieurs séances de sensibilisation ont été organisées afin d'aider les communautés à mieux comprendre les causes des conflits et à les prévenir Le Président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de la commune de Dialgaye, Nogwaya Joseph Sawadogo est revenu sur les principaux conflits enregistrés dans sa commune ainsi que sur les mécanismes locaux de prévention et de règlement. Le PDS a souligné que les conflits les plus récurrents dans notre département sont d'abord les conflits fonciers. « Nous enregistrons également des conflits de limites entre villages administratifs d'un même département, ainsi que des différends entre certaines localités de notre département et les communes voisines, notamment Tensobtenga dans le Kourittenga et des localités relevant de la province du Boulgou», a-t-il indiqué. Il a précisé que l'ODPREGEC, créé en 2015, regroupe les autorités coutumières, les services techniques de l'agriculture, de l'élevage et de l'environnement, les représentants des confessions religieuses, les organisations de la société civile ainsi que les ONG intervenant dans le développement. « Malgré la complexité des conflits fonciers, ces dispositifs nous ont permis d'obtenir des résultats encourageants. Nous avons également mis en place des mécanismes endogènes de prévention et de gestion des conflits », a-t-il précisé. Le Haut-commissaire de la province du Kourittenga, Moctar Ilboudo, a appelé les populations au dialogue et au respect des mécanismes de règlement des différends. « Nous enregistrons principalement des conflits entre agriculteurs et éleveurs ainsi que des contestations liées au foncier. Ces conflits sont inhérents à la vie en société, mais ils doivent être gérés avec responsabilité afin de permettre à chacun d'exploiter paisiblement les terres disponibles», a-t-il déclaré. Il a invité les populations à faire preuve de retenue, à privilégier le dialogue et à recourir aux mécanismes institutionnels et communautaires existants afin d'identifier les causes des conflits et de parvenir à des solutions apaisées. Agence d’information du Burkina AWS/HB/OO

items.title: Grand Prix littéraire Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba : Abdou Lahad Gueye sacré pour « Al Mashrabu’ Ç-Çâfî »
items.description: Le Grand Prix littéraire Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba a livré son verdict. L’ouvrage « Al Mashrabu’ Ç-Çâfî » (« La Source pure ») – Lectures et méditations mourides, écrit par Abdou Lahad Gueye, s’est vu décerner la prestigieuse distinction à l’issue de la cérémonie officielle de remise des prix. Publié en 2026, le livre s’inscrit dans une démarche de transmission et de valorisation de l’héritage spirituel de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. Il trouve son origine dans les séances du Machrab « La source pure » initiées par Serigne Mouhamadou Mountakha Mbacké, Khalife général des Mourides. Une plongée méditative dans les qassidas L’ouvrage rassemble plusieurs lectures et méditations inspirées des qassidas de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba, notamment celles déclamées quotidiennement durant le mois de Ramadan. L’auteur ne revendique ni une exégèse des textes ni une interprétation savante de l’œuvre du fondateur du mouridisme. Sa démarche se veut plutôt méditative. À travers ses réflexions, il cherche à faire ressortir certains enseignements, messages et échos spirituels contenus dans les écrits du Cheikh. Grand Prix Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba : une distinction pour l’œuvre d’Abdou Lahad Gueye Cette approche permet à l’ouvrage de s’adresser à un public relativement large : aux lecteurs déjà familiers des qassidas comme à ceux qui souhaitent découvrir ou approfondir leur connaissance de l’héritage spirituel mouride. « Éclats d’encre au service du Khadim » Le livre est organisé autour de deux grandes parties. La première est consacrée aux lectures méditatives des qassidas. La seconde, intitulée « Éclats d’encre au service du Khadim », aborde plusieurs thèmes liés à la pensée et à l’enseignement de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. L’auteur y revient notamment sur des questions telles que le Ramadan, la repentance ou encore la commémoration de la naissance du Prophète Muhammad ﷺ. Ces différents thèmes sont traités dans une perspective de réflexion spirituelle et de transmission. Une distinction pour un travail de transmission À travers cette récompense, le jury du Grand Prix littéraire Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba distingue ainsi une œuvre qui participe à la diffusion du patrimoine spirituel mouride sous une forme accessible et contemporaine. Pour Abdou Lahad Gueye, juriste, écrivain et blogueur, cette distinction vient également consacrer un travail consacré à la lecture, à l’écriture et à la valorisation de l’héritage de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. Avec Al Mashrabu' Ç-Çâfî, l’auteur propose ainsi une autre manière d’aborder les qassidas : non seulement comme des œuvres poétiques et spirituelles, mais aussi comme une source de méditation et de réflexion pour le lecteur contemporain. C.G. DIOP

items.title: Iran says Pak-Saudi-Turkiye deal shows 'change in perception' towards US
items.description: Iran’s foreign ministry said on Monday that the defence pact signed last week between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye was “a sign of a change in the perception” of regional countries towards the United States. The joint defence agreement, signed in Makkah on Friday, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empowers its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. “This development is a sign of a change in the perception of the countries of the region,” ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said while responding to a query during a weekly press briefing on Monday. “Considering the developments of the last two to three years, the countries of the region have realised that security is not a commodity that can be bought from false security brokers,” Iran’s state media quoted him as saying, referring to the United States. Baqaei further said that there was “no reason to worry that this treaty will be against Iran”, highlighting Iran’s deep religious, historical and civilisational ties with Pakistan, Turkiye and even Saudi Arabia. “This development is an important sign that the countries of the region have concluded that they cannot rely on and trust the claim of security provided by the United States and some other actors outside the region, and they are attempting to try another method; by relying on their own capabilities and perspectives,” IRNA quoted Baqaei as saying. “Any plan that is based on the geopolitical and historical realities of the region, is comprehensive and inclusive, and correctly identifies the enemy and the threat, has a chance of helping to strengthen security and prevent instability and abuses by the Zionist enemy and its allies,” he added, referring to Israel. In response to a question about Iran’s willingness to possibly join the joint pact, Baqaei said Iran has always “emphasised pursuing security mechanisms based on cooperation between regional countries” and “free from the influence and destructive intervention” of foreign actors. “Those plans still exist and can certainly be updated in light of developments,” the spokesperson added. “We are in close contact with neighbouring countries and regional countries, and we hope that all countries will learn from the developments of the last two or three years and adopt the best path to strengthen the region’s collective security,” he said, according to IRNA . Asked about Pakistan’s invitations to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to visit Pakistan, Baqaei said, “This visit will take place whenever the time is right. Bilateral relations are mainly considered.” He added: “The relationship between Iran and Pakistan is a very important one. In the last seven or eight months, it has become even more important than before, for various reasons.” On Sunday, Deputy Prime Minister and FM Ishaq Dar said that the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement remained “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles after the Turkish foreign minister said Egypt could be joining the pact. Dar said the pact was the “culmination of years of discussions and coordination”, adding that it was “purely defensive” in nature. “It is not targeted against any country and its sole purpose is to further strengthen our ongoing efforts towards peace, stability and prosperity in the wider region.” The deputy PM clarified that the pact did not abrogate or replace any existing bilateral or multilateral agreements between the signatory countries, or with other countries or organisations. Dar speaks with Kuwait FM, others on pact Separately, DPM Dar received a phone call from Kuwait’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, wherein the latter felicitated the former on the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Monday. According to the FO, the two dignitaries spoke late on Sunday and also “exchanged views on the regional situation, including occupied East Jerusalem”. They also discussed bilateral relations between the two countries and “matters of mutual interest, including the follow-up to FM Jarrah’s recent visit to Pakistan and further enhancing cooperation and investment in key sectors”. “The two sides agreed to remain closely engaged,” the FO added. The deputy premier also shared the contours of the pact with Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi and former Guinea-Bissau president General Umaro Sissoco Embaló. In a joint call with them late last night, Dar shared the agreement’s “significance for strengthening strategic cooperation and contributing to regional peace, stability and security”, FO said. Dar and Tshisekedi also exchanged views on Pakistan-DRC relations and agreed on the importance of further strengthening bilateral cooperation, including through high-level exchanges. DPM Dar had also spoken to Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand a day ago. “The two exchanged views on the regional situation, including the recently signed Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye,” the FO said. It added that Dar shared the “essence of the agreement” and the “joint resolve of the three countries to contribute to regional peace, stability and security”.

items.title: Alternative analyses of Professor Bokpin’s economic concerns
items.description: 1. Is Ghana Really Approaching a “Failed State”? Professor Bokpin’s warning that infrastructure deficits and power challenges risk pushing Ghana towards a “failed state” reflects a legitimate concern. However, this characterisation may exaggerate the severity of Ghana’s current economic and institutional conditions. A failed state is generally defined by the collapse of governmental authority, inability to provide basic services, widespread insecurity (as observed in Somalia or Sudan), and macroeconomic breakdown. In contrast, Ghana’s current trajectory demonstrates declining inflation, ongoing fiscal consolidation, strengthened reserves, and debt restructuring programmes that have improved medium-term sustainability. Furthermore, Ghana maintains democratic stability, attracts foreign investment, and implements significant structural reforms. Although challenges persist, as is the case in even the most industrialised countries, substantial economic difficulties should not be equated with state failure. A more precise assessment is that Ghana faces development and productivity challenges rather than an existential institutional crisis. 2. Does Macroeconomic Stability Matter Less Than Transformation? Professor Bokpin accurately observes that macroeconomic stability alone does not constitute economic transformation. However, transformation is unlikely to occur in the absence of stability. Historical evidence indicates that successful economies first establish macroeconomic foundations before achieving large-scale industrialisation and structural change. Investors are generally unwilling to commit long-term capital when inflation is unstable, exchange rates are volatile, and fiscal deficits are uncontrolled. The relationship between stability and transformation is therefore complementary rather than contradictory. While lower inflation, improved reserves, and debt sustainability do not guarantee prosperity, they establish the conditions necessary for its achievement. As Harvard economist Dani Rodrik has argued, sustained development requires both sound macroeconomic management and deliberate structural transformation policies. Neither is a substitute for the other. 3. Is the Big Push a Debt Risk or a Growth Strategy? Critics contend that large infrastructure programmes may recreate the debt accumulation problems observed in previous administrations. However, the cost of underinvestment can sometimes surpass the cost of investment. Poor road infrastructure increases transportation costs, raises food prices, reduces competitiveness, and discourages industrial activity. Joseph Stiglitz, a Nobel Prize-winning economist, has argued that well-structured infrastructure investments should be evaluated based on their long-term productive returns rather than solely their upfront costs. Productive infrastructure generates future economic output that can support repayment obligations. The central question is not whether Ghana should invest, but whether such investments are commercially, economically, and fiscally viable. 4. Is the 24-Hour Economy Premature? Professor Bokpin’s criticism presumes that a reliable power system must precede the establishment of a 24-hour economy. Alternatively, increased economic activity can justify and finance improvements in energy infrastructure. Major economies typically expand infrastructure in response to growing demand rather than constructing excess capacity in anticipation of future needs. By promoting continuous operations in manufacturing, logistics, agro-processing, healthcare, transport, and digital services, a 24-hour economy can create commercial incentives for new investments in generation, transmission, and distribution systems. In this framework, the policy is not contingent upon a perfect energy supply but serves as a mechanism for generating the economic activity required to support future energy investments. 5. Is the 24-Hour Economy Authority an Unnecessary Bureaucracy? Professor Bokpin has characterised the proposed Authority as duplicative. However, economic transformation programmes frequently fail because no single institution is responsible for coordination. Implementing a 24-hour economy involves multiple sectors, including energy, transport, labour, taxation, security, trade, customs, manufacturing, and local government. Existing ministries tend to prioritise their own sectoral mandates. A central coordinating institution can reduce fragmentation and enhance accountability. Mariana Mazzucato’s research on mission-oriented development highlights that complex national economic transformations require specialised institutional mechanisms capable of coordinating multiple actors around shared objectives. 6. Is Revenue Mobilisation Merely Another Form of Taxation? Professor Bokpin has consistently cautioned against using taxation as a punitive measure that undermines businesses. The NDC’s approach, however, can be interpreted as focusing on broadening the tax base, digitalising collections, reducing leakages, and improving compliance rather than merely increasing rates. In this context, the government seeks to collect more revenue from previously untaxed economic activities while alleviating pressure on compliant businesses. The central policy debate should therefore address how revenue is raised and whether the tax burden is distributed equitably across the economy. 7. Does Economic Data Reflect Real Improvements? One of Professor Bokpin’s most compelling arguments is that citizens assess economic performance based on their daily experiences rather than statistical indicators. While this perspective is valid, it is also important to recognise that improvements in living standards often lag behind macroeconomic gains. For example, reductions in inflation may take several months to translate into significant increases in household purchasing power. Fiscal stabilisation may occur before job creation, rather than simultaneously. Therefore, the absence of immediate household-level improvements should not be interpreted as evidence of policy failure. A more appropriate assessment is whether current policies are establishing the conditions necessary for future job creation, productivity growth, and income expansion. 8. Monetary Easing, Credit Expansion and the Path to Shared Prosperity. Professor Bokpin correctly asserts that economic statistics must ultimately result in improved living standards, stronger businesses, and quality employment. However, a limitation of this critique is the tendency to evaluate economic recovery at a single point in time rather than as an ongoing process with identifiable transmission channels. Economic transformation is not instantaneous. In most economies, macroeconomic improvements initially manifest in indicators such as inflation, foreign reserves, fiscal balances, policy rates, and lending conditions before translating into business expansion, employment creation, and household welfare. The recent decline in inflation has enabled the Bank of Ghana to initiate a gradual monetary easing cycle. As policy rates decrease, commercial banks experience lower funding costs and can reduce lending rates to businesses and households. This process is a fundamental mechanism by which macroeconomic stabilisation affects the real economy. Lower interest rates are particularly significant, as Ghanaian businesses have long identified high borrowing costs as a major barrier to expansion. Reduced financing costs encourage firms to invest in machinery, expand production lines, purchase inventory, open new branches, and hire additional workers. Increased credit availability is also essential. Recent trends in the banking sector indicate a renewed willingness among financial institutions to extend credit to the private sector, following improvements in macroeconomic stability and confidence. This development is particularly significant because private-sector growth, rather than government spending alone, serves as the primary driver of sustainable job creation. From an economic perspective, the sequence is as follows: Macroeconomic stability leads to lower inflation, which enables lower policy rates, resulting in reduced lending rates. This, in turn, increases private-sector borrowing, drives business expansion, creates jobs, and ultimately improves household incomes and living standards. Critics who demand immediate improvements in living conditions are reflecting public sentiment. However, economic literature consistently demonstrates that the effects of monetary easing and increased credit supply are subject to time lags. Businesses generally require time to adjust investment plans, expand operations, and hire additional workers before households experience the resulting benefits. This perspective aligns with the work of development economists such as Joseph Stiglitz and Dani Rodrik, who emphasise that sustainable growth arises when macroeconomic stability fosters an environment conducive to productive private-sector investment and structural transformation, rather than short-term consumption increases. Consequently, while it is reasonable to question whether citizens are experiencing the full benefits of stabilisation, it is premature to conclude that the recovery has failed solely because the transmission from macroeconomic gains to household welfare is incomplete. Economic recoveries are seldom immediate. The critical issue is whether the necessary conditions for employment growth and rising incomes are being established. Current trends indicate that these conditions are being established. Falling inflation (4.6% in July), declining interest rates, stronger bank balance sheets, expanding credit to productive sectors, and improving investor confidence provide a foundation for business growth. If these developments are sustained, they should gradually result in increased production, higher-quality jobs, stronger household purchasing power, and improved livelihoods for Ghanaians. Accordingly, the debate should shift from questioning the importance of macroeconomic stabilisation to considering whether sufficient time and complementary policies are being provided to enable stabilisation to achieve its full developmental impact. Conclusion: Rather than dismissing Professor Bokpin’s concerns, policymakers should regard them as valuable tests of policy effectiveness. Academic scepticism should be applied consistently to both risks and achievements. If government actions warrant scrutiny for their promises, they also merit recognition when measurable progress is achieved. Equating Ghana to a Sudan, Libya, or Somalia is not a realistic statement in my view. The most equitable assessment of Ghana’s economic trajectory is neither uncritical celebration nor excessive pessimism, but a balanced evaluation grounded in evidence, outcomes, and the long-term realities of economic transformation.

items.title: No backdoor meeting can halt Rainbow Coalition, CRP tells Nunieh, others
items.description: Concerned Rivers People (CRP) has said alleged meetings involving former Managing Director of the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC), Mrs Joy Nunieh, Gabriel Pidomson and Dumo Lulu-Briggs will not affect the Rainbow Coalition. The group, in a statement signed by its Publicity Secretary, Sunny Nwagbo, on Sunday, alleged that Nunieh held a meeting with Pidomson and Lulu-Briggs at her residence to discuss issues relating to the coalition. CRP stated the Rainbow Coalition had come to stay and insists no political manoeuvring would stop the coalition or, in its words, “the will of the people.” CRP maintained that the Rainbow Coalition would remain focused on its political objectives despite the alleged meetings. “Let it be known, the Rainbow Coalition has come to stay. These meetings and backdoor politics will not stop the will of the people,” It added, “Also let us quickly send a reminder to Nunieh that she must be in a hurry to have forgotten so soon how she was saved from the pangs of (enemies) while in office. CRP stressed Nunieh to reflect on her previous political experiences, saying it was concerned that she may have forgotten. The post No backdoor meeting can halt Rainbow Coalition, CRP tells Nunieh, others appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Zik Pan-African Award honours Zenith Bank CEO, Adaora Umeoji for transformational leadership
items.description: Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Zenith Bank Plc,Dame Dr. Adaora Umeoji, OON, has been honoured with the Zik Pan-African Award for Transformational Leadership in Banking and Financial Innovation. The award was presented at the 7th Zik International Peace and Leadership Award Lecture in Accra, where the Zik Lecture was delivered by legal practitioner and the Majority Chief Whip in Parliament, Hon. Rockson-Nelson Etse Kwami Dafeamekpor. The recognition celebrates her nearly three decades of banking experience, more than 20 years of executive management experience at Zenith Bank, and her contribution to the transformation and growth of the financial services industry. Under her leadership, Zenith Bank continues to strengthen its position as one of Africa’s leading financial institutions, with the bank also deepening its presence in Ghana. Zenith Bank Ghana currently operates 43 branches across the country, bringing the institution close to the 50-branch mark as it continues to expand its footprint and widen access to banking services. The growing presence of Zenith Bank in Ghana forms part of the institution’s broader strategy of delivering financial services through a model built around three core pillars: People, Technology and Service. According to Dr. Umeoji, these three pillars have remained central to Zenith Bank’s identity and growth since the institution was founded in 1990 by Dr. Jim Ovia, CFR. Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Zenith Bank Plc,Dame Dr. Adaora Umeoji, OON, “He founded Zenith Bank in 1990, on the solid tripod of people, technology and service,” Dr. Umeoji said. She explained that these pillars have helped to inspire purposeful leadership within the Zenith family while nurturing leaders who continue to champion excellence and drive positive change across industries. The People pillar focuses on the development of employees and leadership, while Technology has become a key driver of innovation and improved access to financial services. Service, meanwhile, remains fundamental to the bank’s relationship with its customers and communities. Dr. Umeoji’s leadership credentials are supported by extensive academic, professional and executive experience. She holds a Bachelor’s Degree in Sociology from the University of Jos, a Bachelor’s Degree in Accounting and a First-Class honours degree in Law from Baze University, Abuja. She also holds a Master of Laws from the University of Salford in the United Kingdom and a Master of Business Administration from the University of Calabar. Her academic journey culminated in a Doctorate in Business Administration from Apollos University in the United States, where her research focused on inspirational leadership and its contribution to leadership and people management. Dr. Umeoji has further undertaken executive management programmes at some of the world’s leading business schools. She is an alumna of Harvard Business School, where she completed the Advanced Management Program and obtained certificates in Leading Global Businesses and Strategic Management. She also completed the Global Banking Program at Columbia Business School, Economics for Business at MIT Sloan School of Management and the Strategic Thinking and Management for Competitive Advantage programme at Wharton Business School. She is a Certified Professional Banker of the Chartered Banker Institute, London, and a fellow of several professional institutions, including the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria, the Institute of Credit Administration, the Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Nigeria, the Institute of Chartered Mediators and Conciliators and the Institute of Chartered Secretaries and Administrators of Nigeria. Her professional influence extends beyond the boardroom. Throughout her career, Dr. Umeoji has delivered keynote speeches and lead papers at academic conferences and symposia, contributing to discussions on financial growth, leadership and people management. She has also participated in high-level bankers’ meetings and contributed to strategies aimed at advancing the banking industry and national economic development. Her passion for developing the next generation of leaders has also seen her deliver motivational speeches and support initiatives aimed at mentoring and empowering young people. Beyond banking, Dr. Umeoji has distinguished herself through philanthropy and humanitarian service. She founded the Pink Breath Cancer Care Foundation, which focuses on educating the public, supporting cancer patients and promoting healthcare programmes across Nigeria. She also established the Adorable Foundation to provide education and support for indigent children, particularly the girl-child. Her humanitarian efforts have attracted recognition from organisations including the Nigerian Red Cross, while the Sun Newspaper honoured her with the Humanitarian Service Icon Award in 2023. Dr. Umeoji has also been recognised for her commitment to ethical banking and service. She instituted the Catholic Bankers Association of Nigeria and has been recognised as a Peace Advocate of the United Nations through UNPOLAC. She is also a Lady of the Order of Knights of St. John International and was conferred with the Papal Knight of the Order of St. Sylvester by His Holiness Pope Francis. In 2022, the Federal Government of Nigeria honoured her with the Officer of the Order of the Niger (OON) for her contribution to nation-building. At Zenith Bank, her leadership responsibilities extend across the group’s operations. She is the Chairperson of Zenith Bank UK and Zenith Nominees Limited and serves as a non-executive director on the board of Zenith Bank Ghana. Under her stewardship, that footprint now extends well beyond Africa. Zenith Bank has commissioned a branch in Paris and established operations in Manchester, complementing its subsidiaries in the United Kingdom, Côte d’Ivoire and Kenya, and positioning the institution as an African financial group with a growing international presence. Receiving the Zik Pan-African Award for Transformational Leadership in Banking and Financial Innovation, Dr. Umeoji described the recognition as more than an acknowledgement of her past achievements. “It is not merely a recognition of past achievements, but a renewed call to greater service,” she said. She dedicated the honour to the board, management and workforce of Zenith Bank, while specifically commending the directors and staff of Zenith Bank Ghana for their contribution to strengthening the Zenith brand in the country. She also expressed appreciation to the Government of Ghana for creating what she described as an enabling environment for businesses and investments to thrive. Dr. Umeoji reaffirmed Zenith Bank’s commitment to widening access to financial services, promoting financial inclusion, improving lives and creating lasting value for the people and communities it serves. For Zenith Bank Ghana, the expansion to 43 branches and its approach towards the 50-branch mark represents more than a growth in physical presence. It reflects an effort to take banking services closer to customers while combining human capital, technology and customer-focused service. The bank’s continued expansion is therefore rooted in the same philosophy on which Zenith Bank was established – People, Technology and Service. These three pillars remain at the centre of the institution’s drive for innovation, operational excellence, financial inclusion and sustainable growth across Ghana and the wider African market. As Dr. Umeoji receives the Zik Award for transformational leadership, her recognition also highlights a leadership philosophy that connects institutional growth with people development, technological innovation and quality service principles that continue to shape Zenith Bank’s journey in Ghana, across Africa and globally.

items.title: ADB makes history with maiden CIB Chapter retreat to shape banking future
items.description: The Agricultural Development Bank (ADB PLC) has made another significant mark in Ghana’s banking industry with the first-ever retreat of its Chartered Institute of Bankers (CIB) Chapter, creating a strategic platform to strengthen professionalism, deepen collaboration, and prepare bankers for the rapidly changing future of financial services. Held at Akosombo on 7 th and 8 th August 2026, under the theme “Recharge, Reconnect and Reinvent,” the two-day retreat brought together members of the CIB-ADB Chapter across the country, executives, and industry experts for a blend of professional development, strategic conversations, mentorship, networking, and team-building. The historic retreat was led by the President of the CIB-ADB Chapter who is also the Deputy Managing Director in charge of Services at ADB, Mrs. Sylvia Naa Kwakai Nyante. Participants were honoured to have the Managing Director of ADB, Edward Ato Sarpong, attending as a Special Guest and the Chief Executive Officer of the Chartered Institute of Bankers, Ghana, Robert Dzato, also attending as a Speaker. The initiative underscores ADB’s growing emphasis on developing its human capital and building a new generation of banking professionals equipped with the knowledge, leadership capabilities, ethical grounding, and innovative mindset in line with ADB’s strategic vision of being among the top 3 banks in Ghana, globally admired for its people, processes, and performance. Theme: Recharge, Reconnect, and Reinvent Addressing participants, Mrs. Sylvia Naa Kwakai Nyante said the maiden retreat represents much more than a gathering of professional bankers, describing it as an opportunity for members to reconnect with one another, strengthen professional relationships, and collectively reflect on their role in shaping the future of banking. Mrs. Nyante emphasised that the theme, “Recharge, Reconnect and Reinvent,” speaks directly to the realities of today’s banking environment, where institutions and professionals must continuously adapt to technological advancement, changing customer expectations, emerging risks and increasing competition. According to her, the strength of the CIB-ADB Chapter must ultimately be reflected in the quality of its members, the professional standards they uphold, and the value they bring to ADB and the wider banking industry. “The future of banking will require professionals who are prepared to continuously learn, collaborate and reinvent or reposition themselves. “This retreat provides us with an opportunity to recharge, strengthen the bonds among us and develop the collective capacity required to contribute meaningfully to the transformation of ADB PLC and the banking profession,” Mrs. Nyante said. She noted that building stronger professional relationships among members would also encourage mentorship, knowledge sharing and a greater sense of belonging within the Chapter. ADB PLC Investing in the Future of Its People The Managing Director of ADB, Edward Ato Sarpong, commended the leadership of the CIB-ADB Chapter for introducing the retreat in the banking industry and creating a platform that brings professional development closer to employees. He noted that the transformation of ADB PLC into a stronger, more competitive and customer-focused institution requires deliberate investment in the people who drive the Bank’s strategy. The ADB MD highlighted that while digital technology is rapidly transforming the delivery of financial services, people will remain central to the success of banking institutions. He, therefore, encouraged participants to embrace continuous professional development and remain responsive to emerging trends within the industry. “As banking continues to evolve, the institutions that will lead are those that combine innovation and technology with knowledgeable, ethical and highly motivated people. “Our investment in professional development is therefore an investment in the future of ADB,” the ADB MD stated. Edward Ato Sarpong urged members of the Chapter to translate the knowledge, relationships and ideas developed during the retreat into improved customer experience, stronger teamwork and greater value for the Bank’s stakeholders. Robert Dzato Challenges Bankers to Prepare for the Future The CEO of CIB Ghana, Mr. Robert Dzato, a guest speaker, highlighted the increasingly dynamic nature of the banking profession and the need for practitioners to continually enhance their competencies. He underscored the important role of professional banking education in building a resilient financial sector and challenged bankers to look beyond traditional approaches to banking as digitalisation, artificial intelligence, data analytics and changing customer behaviour redefine the industry. Robert Dzato further encouraged members to uphold the highest standards of professionalism and ethical conduct, noting that trust remains fundamental to banking despite the technological transformation taking place within the sector. “Banking may be changing in the way services are delivered, but professionalism, competence, integrity and trust will remain at the heart of the profession. “The banker of the future must therefore be technically competent, digitally aware, innovative and deeply committed to ethical practice,” Mr. Dzato said. He commended the CIB-ADB Chapter for setting the pace by organizing the first-ever CIB chapter retreat and creating a dedicated platform for professional engagement. Mr. Dzato also encouraged members to take advantage of the Institute’s programmes to continuously upgrade their knowledge and capabilities. From Professional Development to Stronger Human Connections The retreat programme was deliberately designed to combine professional development with human-centred engagement. The opening day featured a welcome and introductory session followed by a Committee Spotlight Session, during which the Welfare, Learning and Development, and Membership Committees highlighted their roles and priorities. A major feature was “The Big Conversation,” which provided a platform for participants to explore the retreat theme and exchange perspectives on professional growth, collaboration and the changing banking landscape. The programme also featured “Sharing the Thrill,” allowing participants to share experiences and stories that have shaped their professional journeys. On the second day, participants engaged with industry leadership through speaker sessions, while executives and committee members of the CIB-ADB Chapter were inducted and sworn into office. The retreat further incorporated feedback and reflection sessions, networking opportunities and social activities, including a talent show and karaoke night, to deepen camaraderie and strengthen relationships among members. A New Chapter for Professional Banking at ADB The maiden CIB-ADB Chapter Retreat represents a major step in strengthening professional banking culture within ADB and creating a sustainable platform for learning, mentorship and leadership development. It also signals a broader recognition that the future competitiveness of financial institutions will depend significantly on their ability to build bold, agile, innovative and highly skilled workforces capable of responding to disruption and creating value for customers. For ADB, the historic gathering reinforces its commitment to building a workforce that is not merely prepared to respond to the future of banking, but empowered to help shape it even far beyond banking.

items.title: 3rd phase of AJK polls: PPP continues to allege rigging as voting under way in Poonch Division's Bagh, Haveli
items.description: The third phase of elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) is currently underway in four constituencies in Poonch Division’s Bagh and Haveli districts, with the PPP alleging rigging in the fresh round of polls as well. Polling began at 8am and will continue until 5pm. Government officials have anticipated clashes in some areas, while the Election Commission has classified most of the 803 polling stations in the four constituencies as either sensitive or highly sensitive. “Apart from the regular police of both districts, we have dispatched an additional 10,300 troops to maintain law and order and provide a fear-free atmosphere to voters,” Election Commission Secretary Raja Mohammad Shakeel told Dawn earlier. Elections are being held across AJK in phases amid tensions between protesters and the authorities. Polling in Mirpur and Muzaff­arabad divisions was held on July 27 and Aug 2, respectively, with the PML-N securing 24 seats. The PPP has only secured 10 seats so far. The third phase of the polls was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division. The division comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, last week the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli due to concerns over the law and order situation. The AJK election commissioner has hinted that polling on the remaining seven constituencies could be held by Aug 20 or 21. Malpractice, rigging allegations Polling in previous phases of the elections was marred by allegations of rigging , scuffles and violence, with the PPP and the PML-N — the main contenders in AJK but allies in the Centre — engaging in a war of words. The PPP has accused the PML-N of rigging and electoral malpractices in the previous phases. It continued to allege rigging in Haveli and Bagh as well. In a series of posts on X, the PPP shared complaints it said it had filed to the Election Commission. In one of the complaints, the PPP alleged that roads leading to the Banni Marasira area had been blocked, where PML-N supporters were illegally stamping ballot papers at 12 polling stations in the LA-15 constituency. “The commission is requested to consider the two acts together rather than separately, because the second is made possible by the first,” the party said, adding that officials, voters, polling agents and party workers were unable to reach the polling stations “to see what is being done inside”. The party also claimed delays in polling at LA-15’s polling station no.87 in Thub. It also alleged that polling at stations no.143 and 144 in Hatala Pader did not commence on time due to the non-arrival of polling staff. The PPP also alleged that its polling agent was “forcibly removed” from LA-15’s station no.158 in Makhdoom Kot. Similarly, PPP’s agents had also been removed from polling stations no.8-14 in Bani Maldhara and PML-N supporters were stamping ballot papers at those stations, the party alleged. At around 12:45, the party claimed on X that workers of Jamaat-i-Islami had gathered to “capture” 26 polling stations in the constituency — nos.31-38, nos.70-79 and nos.180-186. It said the police had initially arrived but then withdrew. “The stations are, therefore, unguarded at this moment, with an organised body assembled against them.” It urged the Election Commission to determine on whose orders police had withdrawn and direct the law enforcers to return to the station. The PPP also posted a blurry video, which it said was of PML-N workers “attacking” the polling station set up at the Boys Middle School in LA-15 Central Bagh. Regarding LA-16, the party claimed that its polling agents were not being allowed inside stations no.119 and 120 while PML-N supporters were stamping ballot papers inside the stations in the agents’ absence. The PPP further alleged delays in polling at stations no.61 and 141 of the constituency. It made similar allegations regarding polling stations no.109 and 110 in LA-16 Bagh-III Sharqi. Moreover, the party accused “armed individuals associated with the PML-N” of opening fire at polling station no.179, Kot Chinalla in the constituency and disrupting the election process. “The polling agents of the PPP have been removed from the station. It is further alleged that ballot papers are being stamped lawfully,” the PPP added. In LA-17, the party alleged that its agents had been “forced out” from the polling station in Mullah Basti, Kahuta City by PML-N workers. PPP Vice President Sherry Rehman expressed reservations after reports of rigging and malpractices emerged, saying that preventing polling agents from entering polling stations in LA-16 raised “serious questions” about the transparency of the election process. In a statement, she demanded that an explanation be sought from the presiding officers of stations nos.119 and 120 on the matter. The senator also called for the Election Commission to take notice of the reports of PPP’s polling agent being removed from station no.158 in LA-15. Rehman further demanded alternative arrangements to compensate for the shortage of polling staff and material, calling on the authorities to ensure that free and transparent elections were held at all polling stations without any disruption. PPP Secretary General Nayyar Bokhari also accused the PML-N of continuing rigging in the third phase of the elections. He highlighted that his party was regularly informing the Election Commission about the alleged rigging via phone. But, “the chief election commissioner and the election commission secretary’s reply to all of our complaints has been that nothing has happened and everything is good,” he claimed. When Dawn approached the Election Commission regarding Bokhari’s claim, Secretary Raja Muhammad Shakeel said any complaint that he or the chief election commissioner received was being attended and responded to, and the Quick Response Force (QRF) was also moved over it. Rathore, two ex-AJK PMs face crucial electoral test In Monday’s polls, AJK Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore, who is from the PPP, and two of his predecessors — Sardar Tanveer Ilyas and Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan — face a battle for political survival as voters head to the polls. Around 238,664 men and 221,707 women are eligible to cast their ballots at 803 polling stations comprising 1,254 polling booths. A total of 82 candidates are in the fray, with LA-14 (Dhirkot) attracting the highest number of candidates at 30 and LA-17 (Haveli) the lowest at nine. In LA-17, Rathore is facing PML-N candidate Mohsin Aziz and independent candidate Khawaja Tariq Saeed, a member of the AJK Council. Rathore and Saeed had been political allies and, under an agreement, had agreed to contest the seat alternately. However, after becoming prime minister, Rathore asked Saeed to step aside in his favour, a request he did not accept, turning the former allies into rivals. Aziz, whose father Chaudhry Mohammad Aziz had won the seat at least three times, draws support from the sizeable Gujjar community. His recent large election rally in Forward Kahuta reportedly surprised his rivals and underscored the strength of his campaign. Saeed, meanwhile, is believed to enjoy the backing of a sizeable section of the Kashmiri community, as well as an alliance of several smaller clans. Rathore, however, remains confident of retaining the seat, citing the performance of his government during his relatively brief tenure as prime minister. The constituency has also witnessed allegations of electoral irregularities on social media, with reports claiming that two presiding officers had been caught manipulating results in favour of Rathore. Shakeel dismissed the allegations but at the same time confirmed that complaints had been received against the two officials and that they had subsequently been relieved of election duties. In LA-15 (Wasti Bagh), ex-PM Ilyas is facing PML-N candidate and former minister Mushtaq Ahmed Minhas, PPP nominee and sitting minister Sardar Ziaul Qamar, and Jamaat-i-Islami candidate retired Brig Dr Mohammad Khan, a respected educationist. Ilyas, who secured a little over 3,300 votes from Upper Neelum in the second phase of the elections, had initially announced a boycott of the third phase. He subsequently reversed the decision and resumed campaigning, claiming that his victory would enable the constituency to “secure either the presidency or prime ministership.” Ilyas and Qamar belong to the same Madiyal tribe, while Brig Khan belongs to the Narma clan and enjoys the support of former JI chief Abdul Rashid Turabi and former adviser Raja Yasin Khan. Minhas has the advantage of belonging to the PML-N, which is poised to form the next government after emerging as the largest party in the elections held so far. His campaign has also stressed the argument that voters should elect a candidate from the party that is set to occupy the government benches rather than send their representative to the opposition. In LA-16 (Sharqi Bagh), former ministers Sardar Mir Akbar and Sardar Qamar Zaman are the principal contenders, representing the PML-N and PPP, respectively. The fourth contest, LA-14 (Dhirkot), has drawn particular attention because of the challenge faced by Sardar Attique, head of the once-dominant Muslim Conference (MC). Attique is reportedly facing a strong challenge from Sajid Iqbal Abbasi of the relatively new Awam Dast-o-Bazu Party. A contractor and philanthropist, Abbasi is said to have spent millions of rupees from his own resources on public welfare projects in the constituency, helping him build a sizeable personal following. Attique, who has represented the constituency successively since 2006, when he first became prime minister, faces an additional challenge in that Abbasi also belongs to the same tribe. Among nearly two dozen other candidates are PML-N’s nominee Raja Faisal Azad and PPP candidate Raja Mubashar Ejaz. While the main contest is seen as being between Attique and Abbasi, the PML-N and PPP nominees are expected to vie for the second runner-up position. Additional reporting by Tariq Naqash

items.title: Bolgatanga Municipal Health Director wants new hospital to tackle overcrowding
items.description: The Bolgatanga Municipal Director of the Ghana Health Service (GHS), Alhaji Alhassan Lawal, has called for the construction of a Municipal Hospital to reduce the growing pressure on the Upper East Regional Hospital. He expressed concern about the municipality’s lack of a hospital to complement the work of the Regional Hospital, which was frequently overcrowded, particularly at its Out-Patient Department (OPD). “Bolgatanga needs a Municipal Hospital so that we can take the burden off the Regional Hospital. Only specialised or higher-level cases should be referred to the Regional Hospital,” he said. Alhaji Lawal made the call while addressing health sector stakeholders at the 2026 Mid-Year Performance Review Meeting of the GHS in the Bolgatanga Municipality. The meeting was held on the theme: “Advancing Free Primary Health Care in Ghana: Strengthening Access, Equity and Quality Service Delivery.” It provided an opportunity for managers of the Service to assess their performance during the period under review and develop strategies to improve healthcare delivery across the municipality. Expressing deep concern over the situation, Alhaji Lawal appealed to the media in the region to intensify advocacy for the establishment of a Municipal Hospital. He noted that the Bolgatanga Health Centre, which currently had a medical officer serving the entire municipality, was in a deplorable condition and lacked the capacity to adequately serve the growing population or reduce the burden on the Regional Hospital, the region’s main referral facility. The Municipal Director further urged the people of Bolgatanga to treat the issue as a priority and advocate for the construction of a municipal hospital. “I think the citizens of Bolgatanga Municipality should also push for a Municipal Hospital,” he said. Although plans are underway to renovate the Bolgatanga Health Centre with support from the Bolgatanga Municipal Assembly, Alhaji Lawal expressed concern about the limited availability of land for future expansion. “We are using the Bolgatanga Health Centre as our Municipal Hospital in the interim because that is where the doctor is. But the place is in a very deplorable state,” he said. Contributing to the call for a Municipal Hospital, Sydney Ageyomah Abilba, the Regional Focal Person for Malaria, who chaired the meeting, stressed the need for a dedicated Municipal Health facility. “We cannot continue to rely on the Regional Hospital. We have primary and secondary health care. We cannot mix the two,” he said. Mr Abilba explained that the Regional Hospital was a referral facility and should not be burdened with the management of minor conditions. “The Regional Hospital is a referral centre and should not be focusing on minor conditions. That is why the Ghana Health Service has primary, secondary and tertiary levels of service delivery,” he stated. He noted that the same level of strong advocacy that led to the establishment of a Passport Office in the region could also help secure the construction of a Municipal Hospital. Mr Abilba expressed optimism that, with the support of the chiefs and people of the municipality, coupled with strong political commitment, a Municipal Hospital could be built to meet the healthcare needs of residents and ultimately reduce the burden on the Regional Hospital.
